recall.minute: Reinforcement learning is an approach to sequential decision-making in which an agent learns by trial and error to maximise cumulative reward. It suits problems with a known but analytically unsolvable model, problems available only as simulations, and problems that can only be learned by interaction. Compared with supervised learning (labelled answers) and unsupervised learning (structure in unlabelled data), RL has no supervisor, decisions are sequential, time matters and feedback is delayed, which creates the credit-assignment problem and the need to balance exploration with exploitation. The agent–environment loop produces S₀, A₀, R₁, S₁, …; the reward for Aₜ is Rₜ₊₁. An RL system has a policy (habit), reward signal (pleasure/pain), value function (judgement) and optional model (imagination). A tic-tac-toe player stores a win probability per board (1 for wins, 0 for losses and draws, 0.5 otherwise), plays greedily with occasional exploration, and backs up V(s) ← V(s) + α[V(s′) − V(s)]; e.g. 0.5 → 0.55 with α = 0.1 and V(s′) = 1. A step size shrinking to zero converges for stationary problems; a constant one tracks change.
